screens.title: Retargeting Animations & Inverse Kinematics
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn two complementary tools that make character animation flexible: retargeting and inverse kinematics. Retargeting lets you apply the same walk, run, or gesture animations from one humanoid asset to another, so a single animation library works across diverse body shapes. Inverse kinematics, or IK, is a procedural technique that adjusts a limb so an end effector — like a hand or foot — reaches a target in the world. Together these systems let you combine authored motion with runtime adaptation. For example, you can retarget a waved animation from a tall model to a short model without reanimating, and then use IK to make the waving hand actually grab a moving object. We will emphasize the Humanoid Avatar as the intermediary that translates standardized motion into model-specific bones, and we will walk through a practical script that sets IK targets inside the Animator’s OnAnimatorIK callback. By the end of the lesson you will be able to retarget a clip between two humanoid models and implement a basic hand IK target that snaps during Play mode. Consider how this changes your pipeline: fewer bespoke animations, more procedural polish.

screens.title: What is Animation Retargeting?
screens.narratorSegment: Animation retargeting is the process of taking motion data created for one humanoid rig and applying it to another humanoid rig with different proportions. In Unity, this works because the Mecanim system builds a Humanoid Avatar — an internal, standardized skeleton — for each model configured as Humanoid. When an animation plays, it drives the avatar instead of raw bones. The avatar then translates those motions to the actual bone transforms of the target model, scaling and remapping rotations so the movement remains recognizable even when limb lengths differ. A concrete example: a walk cycle authored for a tall, slender character can be used on a short, broad character without manual reanimation. Common misconceptions include thinking retargeting simply copies bone rotations; it does not. It maps motions through the avatar so rotation and positional intent are adapted to the target anatomy. Retargeting relies on correct FBX import settings: set the Rig type to Humanoid and verify the avatar mapping (T-pose alignment and bone assignments). If the avatar is misconfigured, the mapping can produce odd limb twists or a failing retarget. Key takeaway: retargeting reduces animation workload but depends on a validated Humanoid Avatar to translate motion reliably.

keyIdea.text: Retargeting maps animations through a Humanoid Avatar so one authored clip can animate many body shapes without redoing the motion.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › What is Retargeting?
Retargeting — concept
Map authored motion to different humanoid anatomies using the Humanoid Avatar as intermediary.
How it works:
  • Author animation for a source model. Unity records animation data in a clip.
  • Both source and target are imported as Humanoid and have avatars.
  • Mecanim maps clip motion to the avatar; the avatar applies adapted motion to each model.
Key Takeaway
Retargeting saves time but requires validated avatars and correct rig settings to avoid artifacts.
Example: Tall Elf → Stocky Orc
Source
Tall Elf Walk
Author performed stride length and arm swing tuned for long limbs. The clip encodes the motion as rotations and curves.
Target
Stocky Orc
Avatar remaps motion so feet land and arms swing, but step height and rotation magnitudes adapt to shorter limb lengths.
Common mistake
Skipping avatar validation. A misaligned T-pose or wrong bone mapping causes unnatural rotations.
Pro tip
Always check the Avatar preview in the Rig import tab and correct bone assignments before relying on retargeted results.

screens.title: Humanoid Avatar: the intermediary
screens.narratorSegment: The Humanoid Avatar is a standardized internal representation of a human skeleton that Unity builds when you set a model's Rig type to Humanoid. It is not the mesh or the model's bone transforms directly; instead, it acts as an intermediary layer that receives animation data and then drives the actual bones of a target model. This intermediary role is important because animation clips are authored against a normalized structure: joint roles like hips, knees, shoulders, and hands. When an animation plays, Mecanim applies its motion to that normalized avatar. The avatar then converts rotations and positional intent to the target model’s bones, compensating for differences such as limb length or bone hierarchy. Concretely, ensure your FBX imports define a proper T-pose, assign the core bones in the Avatar configuration, and validate the avatar preview to confirm correct mapping. Misconceptions often arise when artists think avatars alter scale globally; instead, they reinterpret motion in the context of each model’s anatomy. Key practical note: failed or incomplete mapping in the Avatar setup will produce twisting or missing motion on the target, so always validate before reusing animations.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Humanoid Avatar
How the Avatar translates motion
The avatar maps role-based joint motion to the model’s specific bones and proportions.
Make sure to:
  • Set the FBX Rig type to Humanoid for both source and target.
  • Align a proper T-pose and assign required bones in the Avatar configuration.
  • Use the Avatar validation preview to confirm mapping and detect mismatches.
Common misconception
The avatar doesn’t change authored motion qualitatively; it reinterprets it to match the model’s bone lengths and orientation, not to create new motion shapes by itself.
Avatar checklist
T-pose alignment
Ensure default pose matches the source to avoid offsets in retargeted motion.
Bone mapping
Map hips, spine, arms, legs, head and confirm no missing required bones.
Validation preview
Use the avatar preview to catch flipped bones or wrong orientations.

screens.title: Prepare FBX and Rig Settings
screens.narratorSegment: Retargeting only works when both source and target assets are configured correctly in the Editor. The preparation steps are simple but essential. First, in the FBX import settings open the Rig tab and set Animation Type to Humanoid. This tells Unity to create a Humanoid Avatar for that mesh. Second, open the Avatar configuration and check that the T-pose aligns and that required bones are assigned. Correct any missing or misassigned bones. Third, validate the avatar preview; the preview will highlight mirrored or flipped bones and alert you to problems. Fourth, create a common Animator Controller and add the animation clip as a state. Attach an Animator component to two GameObjects that hold your two humanoid models and assign the same controller. When you run the scene, Unity will play the same state on both characters, and the Avatar mapping will translate the motion. A common mistake is leaving one model as Generic or forgetting to apply the modified Rig import settings. Always re-import or press Apply in the import inspector after changing Rig type. These preparation steps prevent many later headaches and ensure retargeted motion is reliable.

Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Prepare FBX & Rig
Editor checklist for Retargeting
A short process to make retargeting predictable in Play.
  1. Open FBX Importer → Rig tab → set Animation Type to Humanoid and Apply.
  2. Open Avatar Configuration, confirm T-pose and assign core bones (hips, spine, head, shoulders, arms, legs).
  3. Use the Avatar Validation preview to detect misaligned or missing bones; fix and reapply.
  4. Create an Animator Controller, add the clip, attach Animator components to both character parents, and assign the controller to both.
  5. Run the scene and verify both models play the same state; inspect the Animator and Avatar if motion looks wrong.
Example checklist item
If your model was authored in a different bind pose, correct the T-pose alignment before trusting retargeted results.
Quick troubleshooting
Symptom: Arms twist oddly after retarget.
Fix: Check avatar bone orientation, mirror settings, and reassign arm bones.
Symptom: Animation not applied on target.
Fix: Ensure both Animator components reference the same Controller and both rigs are Humanoid.
Key Takeaway
Small import misconfigurations break retargeting; validate avatars before runtime tests.

screens.title: Retargeting Demo: Play the Same Clip on Two Models
screens.narratorSegment: A quick hands-on demonstration shows retargeting in practice. Create two empty GameObjects in your scene, parent a different humanoid model under each, and name them CharacterA and CharacterB. Attach an Animator component to both parent GameObjects. Create a simple Animator Controller and drag a shared humanoid animation clip such as a 'Wave' into its default state. Assign that Animator Controller to both Animators. When you press Play, both characters should perform the same gesture even if their proportions differ. Use this setup to validate that your Avatar mappings are correct. If one model displays incorrect motion, open that model's Rig tab, confirm Humanoid rig type, and review the Avatar mapping and T-pose. This demo highlights a key benefit: you can maintain one animation asset and deploy it across many characters, dramatically reducing animation asset count. Keep in mind retargeting adapts motion to anatomy but doesn't replace careful posing for character-specific interactions. Retargeting is most effective for general locomotion and common gestures; for very character-specific movements you may still author custom animation. In practical terms, create two characters and one animator controller to observe retargeting in action.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Retargeting Demo
Steps to reproduce
Follow these Editor steps to see retargeting live in Play mode.
  1. Create CharacterA and CharacterB empty parents and place different humanoid models under each.
  2. Add Animator components to both parents and assign the same Animator Controller.
  3. Drag a humanoid animation clip into the controller as a state, save and press Play.

Scenario note
Use this pattern during early prototyping to test how a single animation fits multiple characters before committing to custom clips.
Example observation
If foot placement looks too high on the short model, retargeting may need to be combined with IK foot placement to correct contact points.
Tip
Retarget for general motion; reserve IK or custom clips for precise interactions like grabbing or precise foot planting.

screens.title: Forward Kinematics vs Inverse Kinematics
screens.narratorSegment: Forward Kinematics and Inverse Kinematics are complementary methods for posing joints. In Forward Kinematics, you rotate parent joints and the children follow; it's predictable and artist-driven, ideal for authored clips where every joint is keyed. A simple example is animating an arm: you rotate the shoulder, then the elbow, then the wrist to create a reach. Inverse Kinematics reverses this: you specify the desired position for the end effector — the hand or foot — and the IK solver calculates the joint rotations needed to reach that position. This is invaluable when interactions depend on world position, like placing a foot on uneven ground or having a hand contact a moving object. A misconception is that IK replaces all authored animation; it does not. IK is typically layered on top of existing animation to correct pose in specific situations. Use FK when you need full, artist-controlled motion and precise joint curves; use IK when the scene needs procedural placement or when infinite authored variants would be impractical. The optimal workflow often combines both: author base motions with FK, then apply IK selectively to adapt to the environment.

keyIdea.title: FK vs IK
keyIdea.text: FK is artist-driven joint rotation; IK is target-driven end effector placement. Use FK for authored motion, IK for environment-driven correction.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › FK vs IK
Forward Kinematics (FK)
Animate by rotating parent bones; children follow. Best for authored, precise motion.
  • Artist controls joint-by-joint rotation.
  • Predictable curves and polish for full-body actions.
  • Poor at dynamic environment contacts without many variants.
Inverse Kinematics (IK)
Define where an end effector should be; solver computes joint rotations to reach it.
  • Great for foot placement, grabbing, aiming, and look-at behavior.
  • Works atop existing animations by adjusting specific limbs.
  • Requires care with target reachability and pole vectors for stable bending.
Practical pattern
Author base motion using FK. Apply IK to hands/feet/head to adapt to runtime objects and terrain. This limits the number of bespoke clips while keeping interactions realistic.

screens.title: Common IK Use-Cases
screens.narratorSegment: IK shines when characters must adapt to a changing world. One common case is foot placement: during locomotion on uneven terrain, raycasts under each foot find the ground height and you set IK goals for foot positions so the solver bends the leg to plant the foot. This avoids sliding or floating feet without creating many walk variations. Another use is hand interaction: place a target on an object handle or button and drive the hand target there so the character's fingers or palm contact the object correctly. Head tracking or look-at behavior is also trivial with IK weights for the head to smoothly follow a moving object. Weapon aiming uses IK to keep a weapon aligned to a target while body motion continues from an animation. A key practical point: IK should be constrained to a reasonable anatomical range; unreachable targets produce distortion. Also remember to blend IK with existing animation by adjusting weights. A misconception is pushing IK to handle full-body balance; in most cases, it is best to limit IK to specific chains and combine it with animation layers for stability.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › IK Use-Cases
Practical IK scenarios
Examples where IK reduces animation overhead and increases realism.
Foot Placement
Raycast to find ground under the foot, set IK goal to that position, and adjust foot rotation to match the surface normal for stable planting.
Hand Interaction
Attach a target to an object handle or button and set the hand IK target so fingers and palm meet the object reliably during motion.
Head Tracking
Use look-at weights to smoothly rotate the head toward a moving interest point without modifying body animation significantly.
Weapon Aiming
Drive hand and upper-body IK goals so the weapon aligns to a target while base movement remains driven by clips.
Practical caution
Clamp IK targets and blend weights to avoid limbs snapping or stretching when targets jump or move outside reach.

screens.title: Animator IK API and OnAnimatorIK
screens.narratorSegment: Unity provides IK control points through the Animator component and a script callback named OnAnimatorIK. This callback is invoked during the animation update so you can inject procedural adjustments before the frame renders. Inside OnAnimatorIK you can set IK positions and rotations for AvatarIKGoal entries such as RightHand or LeftFoot, and you can specify weights that determine how much IK overrides the authored animation. For example, calling SetIKPositionWeight with a value of 1 instructs the Animator to fully follow the IK target for that limb; a value of 0 preserves the original animation. You can also set a look-at weight and position to have the head follow a moving object. A typical flow is: compute a desired target position (for a foot, use a raycast to find the ground), clamp it to a reachable range, then call SetIKPosition, SetIKRotation, and the corresponding weight setters. Remember to reset weights when IK is inactive. A common bug is forgetting to set weights, leaving the IK calls ineffective, or assigning unreachable targets which produce distorted limbs. Always test by toggling IK in Play mode to confirm behavior.

A typical flow is: compute a desired target position (for a foot, use a raycast to find the ground), clamp it to a reachable range, then call SetIKPosition, SetIKRotation, and the corresponding weight setters. Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › CharacterIKController
Code panel
Read-only walkthrough: attach the script to your character parent and assign the RightHandTarget.
using UnityEngine;

[RequireComponent(typeof(Animator))]
public class CharacterIKController : MonoBehaviour
{
    protected Animator animator;

    public bool ikActive = false;
    public Transform rightHandTarget = null;
    public Transform lookAtObj = null;

    void Start()
    {
        animator = GetComponent<Animator>();
    }

    // A callback for calculating IK
    void OnAnimatorIK()
    {
        if (animator)
        {
            if (ikActive)
            {
                // Set the look at weight and position (optional)
                if (lookAtObj != null)
                {
                    animator.SetLookAtWeight(1.0f);
                    animator.SetLookAtPosition(lookAtObj.position);
                }

                // Set the right hand target position and rotation, and weight
                if (rightHandTarget != null)
                {
                    animator.SetIKPositionWeight(AvatarIKGoal.RightHand, 1f);
                    animator.SetIKRotationWeight(AvatarIKGoal.RightHand, 1f);
                    animator.SetIKPosition(AvatarIKGoal.RightHand, rightHandTarget.position);
                    animator.SetIKRotation(AvatarIKGoal.RightHand, rightHandTarget.rotation);
                }
            }
            else
            {
                // If IK is not active, reset the weights
                animator.SetIKPositionWeight(AvatarIKGoal.RightHand, 0f);
                animator.SetIKRotationWeight(AvatarIKGoal.RightHand, 0f);
                animator.SetLookAtWeight(0f); // Also reset look at weight if used
            }
        }
    }

    // Optional: Toggle IK with a key press for testing
    void Update()
    {
        if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.I)) // Press 'I' to toggle IK
        {
            ikActive = !ikActive;
            Debug.Log("IK Active: " + ikActive);
        }
    }
}
Explanation
Start caches the Animator. OnAnimatorIK sets targets and weights each frame when ikActive is true; otherwise it resets weights so animation drives the limb.
Example usage
Create a RightHandTarget as a child, assign it in the Inspector, press Play, toggle IK, and move the target to watch the hand snap to it.
Key Takeaway
The script demonstrates a minimal, safe IK pattern: set weights, set positions, and reset when done.

screens.title: IK Pitfalls: Weights, Reach, and Pole Vectors
screens.narratorSegment: When implementing IK you'll encounter a few recurring issues. First, forgetting to set IK weights is a very common one: if weights are left at zero, your SetIKPosition calls will have no visible effect because animation continues to drive the limb. Always confirm that SetIKPositionWeight and SetIKRotationWeight are set to the intended blend. Second, unreachable targets lead to stretching or distorted limb poses. To avoid this, clamp IK targets to a range the limb can physically reach or implement fallback positions when raycasts find no ground. Third, the pole vector problem appears when the intermediate joint, like an elbow or knee, bends ambiguously; without guidance the solver may flip the joint into an unnatural direction. Use SetIKHintPosition to provide a pole vector hint that nudges the elbow or knee into the expected bending direction. A practical debugging flow is: verify weights, visualize target positions, clamp reach, and set hints. Also test toggling IK on and off to ensure weights reset properly. These checks will keep IK stable and prevent the visual glitches that break immersion. Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › IK Pitfalls
Checklist to diagnose IK issues
A short list of symptoms and fixes to stabilize IK behavior.
Symptom: IK has no effect.
Fix: Ensure IK weights are set and not being overwritten elsewhere.
Symptom: Limbs stretch toward target.
Fix: Clamp target distance to anatomical reach or use a fallback pose.
Symptom: Elbow/knee flips.
Fix: Set IK hint positions (pole vectors) to guide intermediate joint bending.
Debug tip
Visualize target transforms in the Scene view and step through OnAnimatorIK with logging to confirm values each frame.
Pole vector guide
Place a hint Transform in front of the elbow or knee direction you want. Use animator.SetIKHintPosition and SetIKHintPositionWeight to apply it.
Takeaway
Stability comes from validating weights, reachability, and hints; treat IK like a constrained solver rather than a magic position tool.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn two complementary tools that make character animation flexible: retargeting and inverse kinematics. Retargeting lets you apply the same walk, run, or gesture animations from one humanoid asset to another, so a single animation library works across diverse body shapes. Inverse kinematics, or IK, is a procedural technique that adjusts a limb so an end effector — like a hand or foot — reaches a target in the world. Together these systems let you combine authored motion with runtime adaptation. For example, you can retarget a waved animation from a tall model to a short model without reanimating, and then use IK to make the waving hand actually grab a moving object. We will emphasize the Humanoid Avatar as the intermediary that translates standardized motion into model-specific bones, and we will walk through a practical script that sets IK targets inside the Animator’s OnAnimatorIK callback. By the end of the lesson you will be able to retarget a clip between two humanoid models and implement a basic hand IK target that snaps during Play mode. Consider how this changes your pipeline: fewer bespoke animations, more procedural polish.

These objectives focus your practice so you can apply retargeting and basic IK in real projects. First, you will understand the concept and benefit of animation retargeting: how a single animation library can serve many humanoid characters by using a shared internal skeleton representation. Second, you will be able to successfully retarget a humanoid animation clip between two different models by setting both FBX rigs to Humanoid and configuring their avatars correctly. Third, you will explain what an Inverse Kinematics solver does: it computes joint rotations so an end effector reaches a desired world position. Fourth, you will implement a simple IK control loop in Unity, using the Animator's built-in IK hooks to set target positions and weights. Each objective pairs conceptual understanding with a practical skill, so you can both reason about the systems and execute the typical steps in the Editor. As you work, check that your avatars are aligned in a T-pose and that IK weights are observable when toggled during Play mode. These outcomes reduce wasted reanimation and increase runtime responsiveness for interactive scenarios.

These additional objectives prepare you to avoid common pitfalls and to choose IK where it is most effective. First, you will learn to configure a Humanoid Avatar correctly: aligning a T-pose and mapping bones so Mecanim can translate motions between rigs. Second, you will practice toggling IK weights and understand how weight values blend authored animation with procedural control, letting you gradually hand control over to IK when needed. Third, you will identify scenarios where IK is the better tool than adding bespoke clips, such as dynamic foot placement on uneven terrain or a hand reaching for a moving button. Fourth, you will learn to diagnose common IK issues—unreachable targets, zero weight, or mis-set pole vectors—and apply fixes that stabilize joint bending and avoid distortion. Each of these skills reduces visual errors in runtime animation and increases the responsiveness of characters in interactive scenes. Try to think about a real scene where the same walk must hit different surfaces; that is where these skills pay off directly.

Animation retargeting is the process of taking motion data created for one humanoid rig and applying it to another humanoid rig with different proportions. In Unity, this works because the Mecanim system builds a Humanoid Avatar — an internal, standardized skeleton — for each model configured as Humanoid. When an animation plays, it drives the avatar instead of raw bones. The avatar then translates those motions to the actual bone transforms of the target model, scaling and remapping rotations so the movement remains recognizable even when limb lengths differ. A concrete example: a walk cycle authored for a tall, slender character can be used on a short, broad character without manual reanimation. Common misconceptions include thinking retargeting simply copies bone rotations; it does not. It maps motions through the avatar so rotation and positional intent are adapted to the target anatomy. Retargeting relies on correct FBX import settings: set the Rig type to Humanoid and verify the avatar mapping (T-pose alignment and bone assignments). If the avatar is misconfigured, the mapping can produce odd limb twists or a failing retarget. Key takeaway: retargeting reduces animation workload but depends on a validated Humanoid Avatar to translate motion reliably.

The Humanoid Avatar is a standardized internal representation of a human skeleton that Unity builds when you set a model's Rig type to Humanoid. It is not the mesh or the model's bone transforms directly; instead, it acts as an intermediary layer that receives animation data and then drives the actual bones of a target model. This intermediary role is important because animation clips are authored against a normalized structure: joint roles like hips, knees, shoulders, and hands. When an animation plays, Mecanim applies its motion to that normalized avatar. The avatar then converts rotations and positional intent to the target model’s bones, compensating for differences such as limb length or bone hierarchy. Concretely, ensure your FBX imports define a proper T-pose, assign the core bones in the Avatar configuration, and validate the avatar preview to confirm correct mapping. Misconceptions often arise when artists think avatars alter scale globally; instead, they reinterpret motion in the context of each model’s anatomy. Key practical note: failed or incomplete mapping in the Avatar setup will produce twisting or missing motion on the target, so always validate before reusing animations.

Retargeting only works when both source and target assets are configured correctly in the Editor. The preparation steps are simple but essential. First, in the FBX import settings open the Rig tab and set Animation Type to Humanoid. This tells Unity to create a Humanoid Avatar for that mesh. Second, open the Avatar configuration and check that the T-pose aligns and that required bones are assigned. Correct any missing or misassigned bones. Third, validate the avatar preview; the preview will highlight mirrored or flipped bones and alert you to problems. Fourth, create a common Animator Controller and add the animation clip as a state. Attach an Animator component to two GameObjects that hold your two humanoid models and assign the same controller. When you run the scene, Unity will play the same state on both characters, and the Avatar mapping will translate the motion. A common mistake is leaving one model as Generic or forgetting to apply the modified Rig import settings. Always re-import or press Apply in the import inspector after changing Rig type. These preparation steps prevent many later headaches and ensure retargeted motion is reliable.

A quick hands-on demonstration shows retargeting in practice. Create two empty GameObjects in your scene, parent a different humanoid model under each, and name them CharacterA and CharacterB. Attach an Animator component to both parent GameObjects. Create a simple Animator Controller and drag a shared humanoid animation clip such as a 'Wave' into its default state. Assign that Animator Controller to both Animators. When you press Play, both characters should perform the same gesture even if their proportions differ. Use this setup to validate that your Avatar mappings are correct. If one model displays incorrect motion, open that model's Rig tab, confirm Humanoid rig type, and review the Avatar mapping and T-pose. This demo highlights a key benefit: you can maintain one animation asset and deploy it across many characters, dramatically reducing animation asset count. Keep in mind retargeting adapts motion to anatomy but doesn't replace careful posing for character-specific interactions. Retargeting is most effective for general locomotion and common gestures; for very character-specific movements you may still author custom animation. In practical terms, create two characters and one animator controller to observe retargeting in action.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Forward Kinematics and Inverse Kinematics are complementary methods for posing joints. In Forward Kinematics, you rotate parent joints and the children follow; it's predictable and artist-driven, ideal for authored clips where every joint is keyed. A simple example is animating an arm: you rotate the shoulder, then the elbow, then the wrist to create a reach. Inverse Kinematics reverses this: you specify the desired position for the end effector — the hand or foot — and the IK solver calculates the joint rotations needed to reach that position. This is invaluable when interactions depend on world position, like placing a foot on uneven ground or having a hand contact a moving object. A misconception is that IK replaces all authored animation; it does not. IK is typically layered on top of existing animation to correct pose in specific situations. Use FK when you need full, artist-controlled motion and precise joint curves; use IK when the scene needs procedural placement or when infinite authored variants would be impractical. The optimal workflow often combines both: author base motions with FK, then apply IK selectively to adapt to the environment.

IK shines when characters must adapt to a changing world. One common case is foot placement: during locomotion on uneven terrain, raycasts under each foot find the ground height and you set IK goals for foot positions so the solver bends the leg to plant the foot. This avoids sliding or floating feet without creating many walk variations. Another use is hand interaction: place a target on an object handle or button and drive the hand target there so the character's fingers or palm contact the object correctly. Head tracking or look-at behavior is also trivial with IK weights for the head to smoothly follow a moving object. Weapon aiming uses IK to keep a weapon aligned to a target while body motion continues from an animation. A key practical point: IK should be constrained to a reasonable anatomical range; unreachable targets produce distortion. Also remember to blend IK with existing animation by adjusting weights. A misconception is pushing IK to handle full-body balance; in most cases, it is best to limit IK to specific chains and combine it with animation layers for stability.

Unity provides IK control points through the Animator component and a script callback named OnAnimatorIK. This callback is invoked during the animation update so you can inject procedural adjustments before the frame renders. Remember to reset weights when IK is inactive. A common bug is forgetting to set weights, leaving the IK calls ineffective, or assigning unreachable targets which produce distorted limbs. Always test by toggling IK in Play mode to confirm behavior.

This pattern is ideal for many simple interactions where only one limb needs procedural control.

When implementing IK you'll encounter a few recurring issues. First, forgetting to set IK weights is a very common one: if weights are left at zero, your SetIKPosition calls will have no visible effect because animation continues to drive the limb. Always confirm that SetIKPositionWeight and SetIKRotationWeight are set to the intended blend. Second, unreachable targets lead to stretching or distorted limb poses. To avoid this, clamp IK targets to a range the limb can physically reach or implement fallback positions when raycasts find no ground. Third, the pole vector problem appears when the intermediate joint, like an elbow or knee, bends ambiguously; without guidance the solver may flip the joint into an unnatural direction. Use SetIKHintPosition to provide a pole vector hint that nudges the elbow or knee into the expected bending direction. A practical debugging flow is: verify weights, visualize target positions, clamp reach, and set hints. Also test toggling IK on and off to ensure weights reset properly. These checks will keep IK stable and prevent the visual glitches that break immersion.
